Lesson 10 · Business route

Difference-in-differences and design threats

Did a facility rollout improve performance beyond the trend already underway?

The business problem

A service network introduced a new scheduling protocol at selected facilities. Performance rose afterward, and the operations director wants to expand it. Other facilities also changed over the same period, so the team compares both groups before and after rollout. The decision depends on the improvement beyond the movement already occurring across the network, together with the cost of training and disruption.

What the data show

The treated group's before–after change minus the comparison group's change is 2.78 index points. The calculation removes a stable level gap, but depends on a credible untreated trend.

The four averages make the calculation visible: adopter performance before and after, and comparison performance before and after. Subtract the comparison group’s change from the adopters’ change to estimate the additional improvement. This approach uses the comparison facilities as a picture of the wider trend. The director should check the actual start of training, whether other sites copied the practice, and whether a separate change reached adopters at the same time.

What would you decide?

Check rollout timing, comparison facilities, spillovers and changing participation before presenting the contrast as a policy effect.

Compare the additional improvement with the minimum gain needed to justify implementation. Review the facility timeline with operations staff, including staffing changes and the sites that remain in the report. If the comparison fits the rollout history, expand in stages under a recorded timetable and track the same outcome for new sites. This creates a practical way to update the decision as implementation proceeds.

Pause and explain

Do similar pre-rollout trends prove that the groups would have moved together afterward?

Compare your reasoning

No. They can challenge a bad comparison, but the treated group’s post-rollout untreated path remains unobserved.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The generator's average effect among adopters is 2.68 points. The difference from the estimated contrast reflects this finite realization of untreated noise.

The bigger picture

A rising outcome after a rollout does not by itself tell a director what the rollout contributed. The comparison must account for the change already happening elsewhere, then connect the remaining gain to implementation cost and a scaling plan. The four-cell table makes that reasoning visible to operations staff. Across the course, the recurring discipline is the same: define the business action, build a comparison that speaks to it, read the result in useful units, and decide what to do next.
